analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin out-of-pocket costs at $35 a month for people with private insurance and covers uninsured users' costs above $35.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support and referred to the Senate Health Committee, the bill never received a vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cap what privately insured people pay out of pocket for insulin at $35 for a month's supply, or 25% of the drug's negotiated price if that is lower, with no deductible applying. It would also create a program where pharmacies and doctors provide insulin to people without insurance, and the government reimburses them for anything above $35 that the patient would otherwise owe. It was referred to the Senate Health Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly several million Americans who buy insulin through employer plans, the individual market, or high-deductible plans, who today can face hundreds of dollars in out-of-pocket costs before coverage kicks in; and uninsured people with diabetes, who would get a guaranteed $35 ceiling through a new federal program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insulin users with private insurance, plus uninsured diabetics

how_it_helps.text: Caps cost-sharing for a 30-day insulin supply at the lesser of $35 or 25% of the drug's negotiated price (net of rebates and other price concessions), starting in 2024, for group plans, individual plans, and catastrophic plans.
Eliminates any deductible for selected insulin products, so patients get the cap from day one rather than after meeting a deductible that can run into the thousands.
Requires the cap to count toward the plan's deductible and out-of-pocket maximum, so it doesn't strand patients outside other protections.

Creates a program where pharmacies and health care providers furnish insulin to uninsured individuals and HHS pays the difference between the patient's out-of-pocket cost and $35, with the provider barred from billing the patient for that amount.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and self-insured employers absorb the gap between the $35 patient cap and the insulin's actual price, which could be passed into premiums for all enrollees. Federal taxpayers fund the reimbursement program for the uninsured. Insulin manufacturers largely keep their prices, since the cap limits what patients pay, not what the drug costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps what patients pay, not what insulin costs: insurers pay the remainder of the drug's price, which could show up as higher premiums for everyone rather than pressure on drug makers to lower prices.
Insurers only have to offer the cap for one 'selected' insulin product of each type and dosage form, and they choose which ones; insulin obtained out-of-network can still carry higher cost-sharing.
The bill provides no funding offset; it includes only a non-binding statement that a future Congress should find one, leaving the uninsured-coverage program's cost open-ended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and immediate for insulin users, a group for whom rationing medication can be life-threatening. The main cost is that the burden shifts to premiums and federal spending instead of attacking list prices directly. It is a patient-protection bill rather than a drug-price bill, and it would have been genuinely helpful to people rationing insulin, though a bill targeting manufacturer prices would have gone further.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never voted it out, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Raphael Warnock introduced the bill on March 23, 2023, together with Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where no markup or vote ever occurred.
Eleven senators cosponsored it, split 6 Republicans and 5 Democrats.
The only action after referral was a Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee hearing on November 30, 2023 (printed as S.Hrg. 118-511), which was not a vote on the bill.
No further action was taken, and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, self-insured employers, and insulin manufacturers are better off: none of them took on the cost-sharing obligation the bill would have imposed. Americans who ration insulin because of its out-of-pocket cost gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and insulin makers avoided the mandate

for.name: Sen. Raphael Warnock
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled bipartisan cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its Republican co-lead at introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee the bill was referred to never reported it to the floor or scheduled a markup; no vote was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 6 Republicans and 5 Democrats joined the sponsor — but because no vote was ever recorded, where the chamber actually stood is unknown.

industries.note: They would pay the difference between the $35 patient cap and the insulin's negotiated price, and could shift that into premiums. The bill's core requirement lands directly on them.
The bill caps what patients pay but not what the drug costs, so manufacturers' revenue is largely preserved while the appearance of affordability improves. It does not force price cuts at the source.
They would be reimbursed by HHS for insulin they furnish to uninsured patients above the $35 patient ceiling, and are barred from billing the patient for it.
